units.title: High-throughput chains with modified gas models
angles: Arithmetic and control flow. Read the interpreter this network runs at the release its endpoint reports, and any compiler, bytecode rewriting, caching or code analysis stage in front of it. Cover the 256 bit integer library and its pinned version, MULMOD, ADDMOD, DIV, SDIV, MOD, SMOD, SIGNEXTEND, SAR, SHL, SHR, BYTE, EXP, the comparisons, JUMP and JUMPI with the jump destination analysis, KECCAK256, MCOPY, memory expansion and CALLDATALOAD. Compare each with the Ethereum specification at the edges that OPCODES.md lists, and read the release notes and fix commits since the versions OPCODES.md records. Then rerun the scripts in research/network-risk/tools/opdiff (battery.py, targeted.py, pmdiff.py, pmdiff2.py, swaps.py, replay.py) for this unit's chain ids, write the outputs into your work directory, and add vectors for anything the reading makes suspicious. Report every result that differs from the specification, every release that changed these paths, how a wrong result would change the pool math in src/libraries (TickMath, BitMath, FullMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, TickBitmap) or the logic that depends on it, and which validators could run a different code path than the public endpoint.

Known weaknesses. Collect security advisories, audit reports, bug bounty write-ups, incident post-mortems and open issues for this network's execution client, precompiles and system contracts from the last two years, including behaviour the network calls by design. For each, decide whether an ordinary account could use it against funds in the PoolManager.

code.task: The owner of the review has allowed the Solidity compiler for this work. solc 0.8.26 is installed as a JavaScript package at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-v4-core/0b315df9-4a6b-5032-a881-24bad3c79fc5/scratchpad/solcjs/node_modules/solc (do not install anything else). research/network-risk/tools/build/compile.js shows how to call it with the settings of foundry.toml (optimizer runs 44444444, viaIR, evmVersion cancun, metadata bytecodeHash none) and the remappings; copy it into your work directory and change outputSelection to get what you need (for example 'ir', 'irOptimized', 'evm.assembly', 'evm.deployedBytecode.sourceMap', 'evm.deployedBytecode.functionDebugData', 'evm.legacyAssembly'). The build of this checkout is in research/network-risk/build/PoolManager.json (runtime 24,009 bytes; its creation code hash equals the value in snapshots/PoolManagerTest.json). research/network-risk/tools/opdiff/pyevm.py is a reference EVM in Python that runs the bytecode instruction by instruction and can record which program counters ran; bytecode.py, buildcheck.py and v4math.py show how it is used. Read research/network-risk/OPCODES.md first. Never compare this code or this bytecode with upstream v4-core or with any deployed contract. Task: map the built runtime bytecode to the source and check the compiled form of the arithmetic. Part one: produce a table that assigns every range of the runtime bytecode to a function of the source (dispatcher, each external function of PoolManager and its bases, each internal function or inlined library routine that the debug data or the optimized IR names), and list the ranges that no script of OPCODES.md executes (use pyevm coverage from bytecode.py; the instruction coverage is 77 percent). Part two: for every MULMOD, SDIV, SMOD, SAR, BYTE, EXP, ADDMOD, DIV and MOD instruction in the bytecode, and for a sample of at least 40 of the SIGNEXTEND, SLT, SGT, SHL and SHR instructions chosen across functions, name the source line it implements and check from the optimized IR and the surrounding instructions that the compiled code computes what the source line says at the edges OPCODES.md lists (operand order, the width of the sign extension, shift amounts, the sign of a remainder, division by zero, masking of narrower types before use). The optimizer may have fused, reordered or simplified operations; say where it did and whether the simplification is valid for every input. Part three: find the one EXP and the one ADDMOD in the bytecode and say whether they are code or data and what reaches them. Part four: for each chain-dependent instruction (CALLER, CALLVALUE, ADDRESS, SELFBALANCE, GAS, CALL, STATICCALL, the transient and persistent storage instructions) say which source line it belongs to. Report anything where the compiled code and the source disagree, and anything in the compiled form that would behave differently on a network whose interpreter differs from the specification in one of the ways OPCODES.md discusses.

Task: settle the open leads on the compiler (L-028, L-151, L-152). Part one: read the official Solidity list of known bugs (https://github.com/ethereum/solidity/blob/develop/docs/bugs.json and docs/bugs_by_version.json through raw.githubusercontent.com, and the Solidity blog posts for each entry) and list every bug that applies to version 0.8.26 with the settings of foundry.toml (via IR, optimizer on, Cancun), with its conditions. An earlier cycle named one as SOL-2026-7, published on 2026-10-22, in the Yul optimizer; confirm the entry, its exact trigger and its fix version from the primary source. Part two: for each such bug decide whether the build of this checkout meets the trigger. Use the compiler outputs 'ir' and 'irOptimized' for src/PoolManager.sol and search them for the code shape each bug needs; where a bug description gives a minimal example, compile the example with the installed 0.8.26 to see the faulty output and learn what to look for. Part three: where a bug could apply, find the function of the source it would affect and test that function's compiled behaviour against the source in pyevm (buildcheck.py shows the method for swaps and liquidity; extend it to the function in question). Part four: say what the transient storage, the memory-safe assembly blocks and the use of custom user defined value types and operators in this source mean for each listed bug. Report each bug as affects this build, does not affect this build, or undecided, with the evidence.
